title: Processor, Memory and Data-Movement Architecture

standard.family: AutoLeaP Embedded Systems Body of Knowledge

summary: Processor architecture determines more than instruction throughput. Privilege levels, exception handling, memory protection, cache hierarchy, interconnect, DMA masters and peripheral ownership define the system's isolation and timing behavior. A design that ignores these relationships can be functionally correct in source code and still fail because a device reads stale memory, an interrupt cannot be cleared, or a lower-trust master accesses protected data.
learningObjectives: Explain CPU privilege, cache, MMU/MPU, DMA and interrupt interactions.
Design deterministic and protected memory/data paths.
Identify correctness failures caused by coherency, alignment and ownership errors.
explanation: Processor architecture determines more than instruction throughput. Privilege levels, exception handling, memory protection, cache hierarchy, interconnect, DMA masters and peripheral ownership define the system's isolation and timing behavior. A design that ignores these relationships can be functionally correct in source code and still fail because a device reads stale memory, an interrupt cannot be cleared, or a lower-trust master accesses protected data.

An MPU provides region-based access control, commonly in microcontrollers and RTOS systems. An MMU translates virtual addresses and supports process-oriented isolation and richer operating systems. Neither automatically constrains DMA; an IOMMU or system firewall may be required. Cache reduces average latency but creates coherency and worst-case variability. Tightly coupled memory can provide predictable access for selected code or data.

Data movement needs an explicit ownership protocol. For each shared buffer, the architecture should define producer, consumer, lifetime, cache maintenance, alignment, synchronization and failure behavior. Interrupt design must similarly define source acknowledgement, priority, execution budget and deferred processing. These contracts belong in driver and platform architecture, not only in low-level implementation notes.
whyItMatters: Data-movement bugs are intermittent, load-dependent and difficult to reproduce.
Memory and protection design is a prerequisite for security, real-time timing and mixed-criticality consolidation.
activities: Trace CPU and DMA access paths
Test protection faults, overload and reset recovery
automotiveExample: A camera gateway uses DMA to write frames into DRAM while a Linux process reads them. The driver allocates DMA-safe buffers, synchronizes ownership, and maps only required regions through an IOMMU. A real-time metadata path uses a separate bounded queue so graphics load cannot delay control-state publication.
commonMistakes: Using volatile as a substitute for synchronization or cache maintenance
Assuming CPU memory protection covers all bus masters
Designing from average memory bandwidth instead of contention cases
Clearing only the interrupt controller while the device source remains asserted
Treating linker placement as a build detail rather than architecture
